Orange County has a Real Estate Assessment Department, created in 2024, that sets values. The Treasurer collects the tax. The county explains that Virginia requires real estate to be assessed at 100 percent of fair market value, and that the department exists to spread the tax burden fairly.

OfficeWhat it doesHow to reach it
Real Estate Assessment DepartmentAnnual assessments and appeals intake(540) 672-6173, 112 West Main Street, Orange, VA 22960
TreasurerBills, payments, late payment rulesMain line (540) 672-3313, P.O. Box 111, Orange, VA 22960
Board of EqualizationReviews assessment complaintsThrough the assessment department, (540) 672-6173

For any question about value, call the assessment department.

sections.h2: Due dates and the 2025 billing change
sections.html:
Orange County sends two installments for real estate tax: half is due December 5, and the rest is due June 5.

The county lined its tax year up with its July 1 to June 30 fiscal year. The board adopted the change on October 8, 2024, under Virginia Code 58.1-3010, and a short interim fiscal year ran January 1 to June 30, 2025. You still get a December bill and a June bill, but December is now the first half.

  • September to October: the first bill of the fiscal year goes out, covering the first half.
  • December 5: first half due, based on the January 1 assessment and the rate set the previous spring.
  • Spring: reassessment notices arrive each year.
  • June 5: second half due, resting on the assessment and rate from the prior year's cycle.

A reassessment notice is not a bill. A new value first shows up on the bill due the next December, so a June payment can reflect an older value than the notice in your mailbox. Remember that when you split costs at closing.

Miss a deadline and the penalty is 10 percent of what you owe. Interest of 10 percent a year then builds on the tax and the penalty together. For the December bill it begins December 6 and is added on the first of every month after, citing Code of Virginia 58.1-3916.

Paying by mail works only when the envelope has a Post Office postmark dated on or before the deadline. A postage meter imprint is not accepted in its place.

  • Nobody gets a waiver for a bill that never arrived, an old mailing address, or a misread date.
  • A medically determinable impairment on the due date can qualify for an exception if you pay within 30 days.
  • The penalty does not apply when a mistake by the Treasurer or the Commissioner of the Revenue alone caused the delay.

Selling with an overdue bill means the closing agent must collect a payoff covering the penalty and the interest.

Call the assessment department, submit the county's appeal application, and escalate to the Board of Equalization only if that review leaves you unsatisfied.

The circuit court appoints the board. Its members are mostly local freeholders, and at least 30 percent must be current or former real estate, construction, financial or legal professionals. Its powers come from Chapter 32, Article 14 of Title 58.1, and the notice you receive should say so.

Va. Code 58.1-3379 treats the assessor's number as correct until you show otherwise. County staff say they do not choose values to move tax totals: the market drives value, and the Board of Supervisors fixes the rate each spring. Arrive with comparable sales and photographs of defects, not complaints about the rate.

The tax has first claim on the property, and it is paid from proceeds before the buyer gets clean title.

Va. Code 58.1-3340 lets that lien jump ahead of all others and sends the buyer or foreclosure trustee to pay it from the sale. Splitting the year's tax between the parties is up to the contract. At recording a grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 is due under Va. Code 58.1-802, charged to you as the seller unless the contract says otherwise.

A parcel in the land use program carries a special valuation, so ask the county how a change of ownership affects it. Relief programs exist for older and disabled owners and for disabled ex-service members, each with a separate application.

Most sellers here run into the timing of the two bills and the effect of annual reassessment on the number they see.

  • Parcel size: acreage and land use status can change both the bill and the sale process.
  • Timing: the December and June deadlines can fall in the middle of a contract period.
  • Lag: a new assessed value does not reach a bill until the following December.

Heirs who would rather not repair, show and wait may prefer a direct cash sale. Taxes are settled the same way whatever the buyer, so get a balance from the county first.

The county lies in the central Piedmont, where rolling hills climb toward the Blue Ridge on the west side. It counted 36,254 people in 2020. Orange, the county seat, and Gordonsville are the two incorporated towns. Barboursville and Lake of the Woods are census-designated places, and mailing addresses also use names such as Locust Grove, Rapidan, Rhoadesville, Unionville, Somerset and Montpelier Station. Montpelier, the 2,700-acre estate of James Madison, lies in the county. Because addresses and place names vary, give the Assessment Department your tax map or parcel details when you call.

A short call can save a delayed closing. Ask whether the December bill has been paid in full, whether any penalty or interest has been added, and how the office wants a payoff request submitted. Ask what date the figure is good through, since interest is added on the first of each month. If an estate or a relative is handling the sale, ask what proof of authority the office needs before it will talk about the account.

Do these in order. Get the Treasurer's balance on each open bill and note which half is paid. Set the spring assessment notice next to the value a buyer will find online. If the parcel has acreage, confirm its land use status. Finally, read the proration language in your contract so the December and June bills are split the way you expect. A closing agent can then request one payoff that covers taxes, penalty and interest in a single figure. If the numbers disagree anywhere, such as the Treasurer's balance and the contract's proration, settle the difference before the closing date rather than at the table. Orange County property is often a mix of house and land, so make sure each tax map number tied to the sale is included in the payoff request. A missing parcel is a common reason a payoff comes back short.

faqs.q: When are Orange County real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half comes due December 5 and the second June 5. December is now the first bill of the county's fiscal year.

faqs.q: Does Orange County reassess every year?
faqs.a: Yes. The county conducts annual reassessments, starting in 2025, and mails notices in the spring. Notices are not bills.

faqs.q: Can Orange County waive a late tax penalty?
faqs.a: Rarely. Penalty and interest are not waived for a missed bill or a misread date. Limited exceptions cover a medical impairment and county error.

faqs.q: Who do I call about an Orange County assessment?
faqs.a: Phone the Real Estate Assessment Department, (540) 672-6173, 112 West Main Street in Orange.

faqs.q: Do I pay Orange County property tax when I sell?
faqs.a: Yes, any balance is deducted from proceeds at closing. The year's tax is normally split in the contract.
